thread.title: Apple: How The Mighty Have Fallen - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Victor Dergunov
title: Apple: How The Mighty Have Fallen - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Source: MacRumors.com
Apple ( AAPL ), until recently was perceived as essentially being a bulletproof investment as far as tech stocks. A relatively low valuation hybrid company, combining the best of both worlds, deep value coupled with stable growth.
Naturally, it came as a shock to many market participants when the stock got punished relentlessly in recent weeks. In fact, all the stock’s gains over the past year have been erased, and Apple now sits more than 25% below its all-time high achieved just six weeks ago.
Apple One-Year Chart
Source: StockCahrts.com
Stagnant iPhone sales coupled with sky-high average selling prices ASPs are suggesting that growth in Apple’s core product segment may be about to fizzle out. Given that the company derives roughly 60% of its revenues from iPhone sales, and about another 20% from sluggish Mac and iPad sales, the end of Apple’s growth story is a legitimate concern right now.
After years of having Apple as a top portfolio position I substantially reduced Apple holdings prior to my last article “ Apple: The Demise of a Growth Era .” Nevertheless, the company’s services and “other” segment continue to show robust expansion, and the stock is now more than 25% cheaper than it was just several weeks ago.
The bottom line is that Apple’s stock is beginning to look increasingly more attractive as its price continues to cascade lower, and due to the company’s relatively cheap valuation, Apple is likely to represent a compelling long-term buying opportunity going forward.
The Big Problem Apple Faces After many years of growing iPhone unit sales and subsequently expanding ASPs, Apple appears to be toward the end of its profitability maximization cycle. With the iPhone ASP up by a staggering 29% last quarter , and approaching $800, it's likely that iPhone revenue growth is going to be extremely limited from now on.
With roughly 60% of Apple’s total revenues coming from iPhone sales, this may essentially reduce the company to a “value stock.” This equates to multiple compression, and this is what we’re seeing right now. To exacerbate the problem, Apple’s EPS could conceivably decline going forward if iPhone ASPs fall.
Apple Revenues Breakdown
Source: Statista.com
In a worsening scenario ASPs or unit sales may decline going forward, and in a worst-case scenario both ASPs and unit sales may decline. This would put significant pressure on Apple’s revenues and profits, which would then make the stock appear overpriced, even at current “discounted” prices.
This is the nightmare scenario that long Apple investors face due to the company’s nature as a hardware company and its extreme dependence on iPhone sales. The good news is that a drop off in iPhone revenues probably wouldn’t materialize unless a substantial slowdown or a recession occurred. The bad news, however, is that a recession or a substantial economic downturn is starting to appear more likely.
Apple’s Revenue Streams Unfortunately, services and “other” products will not be enough to offset the iPhone slowdown. The problem for Apple is that the company is selling fewer iPhones than it did in 2015. Granted, they are more expensive now, but unit sales are just not increasing as many had hoped.
iPhone Unit Sales by Quarter
Source: Statista.com
For instance, last quarter Apple saw iPhone revenues surge by 29% on flat unit sales . So, all the gains are simply due to ASPs increasing. This kind of growth is unsustainable, and iPhone revenue growth may stall or even decrease going forward. This is especially true now, as Apple has already introduced its new, higher price lineup.
Another factor that market participants may want to consider is that future upgrade cycles may last longer, as consumers could hold on to their devices for three-to-four years rather than the typical two-years to two-and-a-half years. Prices are extremely high, and capability increases are relatively marginal right now. Therefore, it's quite plausible that YoY unit sales may begin to slip in future quarters and years. In fact, we’re already starting to see the cracks in the iPhone story , as Apple suppliers reduce revenues expectations, pointing to less than stellar demand for the XS Max and XR iPhone variants.
Mac and iPad prospects are not looking great either. The company receives approximately 20% of its sales from Mac and iPad sales and last quarter showed that iPad unit sales declined by 6% YoY, while Mac unit sales missed by 2% YoY. Moreover, iPad revenues dropped by a whopping 15% YoY, showing a falloff in ASPs, while Mac revenues increased by a modest 3% YoY. Also, if we look at full-year sales, iPhone and iPad units were flat for the entire year, and Mac unit sales were down by 5% YoY in fiscal 2018.
Source: Apple 8-K
So, this leaves Apple’s services and “other” segment to make up for the diminishing revenue growth momentum. (“Other” segment includes products like the Apple Watch, Beats headphones, HomePod smart speaker, AirPods, and other accessories).
On a full-year YoY basis services grew at 24% and other expanded by 35% . However, these two segments accounted for only 20% of total sales. Also, if we look at Q4, growth slowed in both segments, services expanded by 17%, and other grew by 31%. Additionally, it's important to point out that “other,” while expanding faster is far smaller than services, and accounted for only 7% of total revenues in Q4.
It's probable that growth will continue to slow into next year, even in these faster growing segments, and combined services and other may deliver growth of around 20% YoY in 2019. However, due to the relatively small percentage of revenues (20%) these units account for, the overall impact on Apple’s revenue growth as a company from services and other will only be about 4%.
Incidentally, consensus analysts are looking for revenue growth of only about 5% this year and just 4% next year. This essentially means that most analysts are not expecting any unit or ASP growth in Apple’s primary hardware segments, iPhone, iPad and Mac, which account for approximately 80% of the company’s revenues. This is a big problem for Apple, and is a primary concern to investors today.
It’s Not All Bad News But enough about the negatives, let’s talk about some good news concerning Apple. While Apple may be entering a challenging period, it's likely going to be a transient phase, and Apple still represents a strong long-term investment going forward.
Apple’s Gigantic Cash Position: Could Generate Growth
Apple reported an enormous stockpile of cash ( $237 billion ) at the end of fiscal 2018. With this kind of cash the company should be able to buy itself a new growth story. Apple may use some of its cash to purchase businesses that may improve the company’s growth prospects, and/or the company can continue to design innovative new products that may unlock future growth scenarios. In addition, the company has the means, so it's likely to continue to buy back stock.
Apple’s Buybacks: Likely to Continue
Back in May Apple announced an enormous $100 billion stock buyback program . Apple reported roughly 5 billion shares at the end of last quarter, a decrease of about 4.8% YoY. As the company continues to buy back stock, it takes shares out of the public market, leaving fewer shares for profits to be distributed to in the form of EPS, effectively making the stock cheaper in the process. With Apple’s massive cash position this trend is likely to continue, which should help establish a floor underneath the stock, and should support higher stock prices going forward.
Apple’s Dividend: Likely to Increase
Although Apple doesn’t provide a massive dividend percentage wise, at more than $13 billion the company distributes the largest dividend dollar wise out of any company in the world right now. The current yield is just 1.5%, but it's going higher as the stock goes lower, and it's likely to be increased going forward as Apple transitions into a more mature value company.
Apple’s Incredible Ecosystem: Should Continue to Expand
Another factor that is likely to keep Apple’s stock afloat in a downturn and supports the idea for a higher stock price longer-term is Apple’s incredible ecosystem. At the beginning of 2018 Apple reported that the company had approximately 1.3 billion active devices worldwide. The company also recently announced that it shipped out its 2 billionth iOS device. App growth also has been exponential with about 180 billion total Apple App Store downloads in 2017.
App Store Downloads
Source: Statista.com
Apple products are extremely sticky despite being relatively costly, and they also are some of the best consumer products ever made. Many people who use Apple’s products are going to continue to use them, and Apple’s massive ecosystem should continue to grow as a result.
The services segment, which currently stands for about 13% of the company’s total revenues, should continue to expand, as it's essentially the driver that keeps Apple’s ecosystem functioning at an optimal level. Therefore, the services segment should continue to grow, continuously becoming a larger portion of the company’s revenues, and powering growth in the future.
Apple’s Valuation: Relatively Cheap Right Now
EPS estimates have come down modestly in recent weeks. 2019 full-year estimates have come down by 29 cents or roughly 2% in the last 30 days. However, if we go out further estimates are only down by about 8 cents over the last three months. Right now, consensus estimates are calling for EPS of $13.48 for full fiscal 2019. Still, the range is rather wide from $11.54 to $15.40. This implies that at its current price ($172) Apple is trading at about 12.75 times this year’s projected earnings (consensus estimates). But it could be trading anywhere from 11 – 15 times this year’s earnings.
Next year’s range is even wider, with lower end estimates sitting at about $11, and higher end estimates going all the way up to $18. This implies that Apple is currently trading between 9.5 – 15.6 times 2020 estimates. Apple is not likely to completely miss consensus analysts’ estimates, so unless a serious recession develops the company should report substantially better than the lower end figures. On the flip side, unless something extremely beneficial or unexpected happens, numbers are not likely to surprise substantially higher either.
Ultimately, the company is likely to hit about the mid-range earnings wise $14.50 next year, in my view. This is slightly lower than the $14.82 consensus figure. $14.50 in EPS equates to a forward P/E of just 11.8, quite low by historical standards, not just for Apple, but for any technology company.
Earnings Risk One risk that should be discussed is if the company's earnings decline due to lower iPhone sales and/or higher costs. In this scenario the current consensus and higher end P/E projections could be somewhat decoupled from reality.
In a lower growth economic environment Apple could earn just $11 this year and the next, possibly even lower. In this case the 15.6 or higher forward P/E multiple would be too high, and the stock could potentially decline more as a result in the short to intermediate term.
The Bottom Line Apple remains an incredibly strong enterprise, and although it's difficult to look at it as a growth company anymore, Apple can still do quite well as a value stock. The value is there, the dividend is there, the buybacks are going to continue, and Apple has a massive pile of cash it can use to possibly propel growth going forward. Additionally, Apple’s services and “other” segments should continue to grow on their own, and will likely continue to add modestly to Apple’s overall growth picture in future years.
Apple’s current valuation is relatively cheap, and despite a slower revenue growth trajectory, an EPS decline seems unlikely going forward. Moreover, the company is likely to resume its EPS growth trajectory after a temporary period of low growth or stagnation. Therefore, the current rout in the stock is very likely a transient phenomenon, and Apple remains a strong buy as a long-term investment.
Ultimately, I expect Apple’s stock price to roll back a bit further (possibly to the $135 - $155 level), especially if an economic downturn becomes more evident. However, Apple begins to look extremely attractive at slightly lower levels, and market participants are likely to step in and bid the stock higher if lower prices materialize.
